comments.author: lucasluitjes

> The current attack is sensitive to network conditions, like RTT and jitter. Low, stable round-trip times are preferred for a more reliable attack. In our controlled environment, we performed this attack over the internet through public IP addresses instead of just assuming perfect laboratory conditions. For the current attack path to achieve optimal stability and reliability in exploitation, Calif turned to physics and utilized money to solve the problem, rather than experimenting with TCP/IP stack configuration. But a long tail of unpatche

comments.author: ievans
comments.text:
Super impressive work by Calif as usual.
The exploit conditions are very specific but there are still going to be a lot of hosts impacted. We at Semgrep published some free detection scripts here:
https://github.com/semgrep/detection-scripts/tree/main/CVE-2...
They look for these five conditions:
* HotSpot VM: any OpenJDK build, Oracle JDK, or GraalVM JDK. Only HotSpot generates the stub. OpenJ9 and GCJ are OK. Azul Prime (Zing), which replaces C2 with its own JIT, and any VM name not recognized as HotSpot are [?], never [!].
* x86-64 JVM on an x86-64 host.
* Version 17.0.6 or later, not at or above a version listed in FIXED_IN, and no newer than the newest releases checked (see below). Newer versions are [?]: they may carry the fix.
* The JVM reports avx512_vbmi and avx512bw, and UseAVX >= 3.
* Base64 intrinsics are on and C2/JVMCI can compile. These turn it off: -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics, -XX:DisableIntrinsic=_base64_decodeBlock, -Xint, -XX:TieredStopAtLevel below 4.

comments.author: tristanj
comments.text:
It's pretty obvious that Gemini 4 Carbon is not token efficient. It also has relatively low tokens-per-second compared to other models. I can think of several reasons why this is the case:
1. Google has huge amounts of cash and compute. Their goal was to train a model that that has the highest quality & frontier performance, not create a model that's efficient to run and serve. They have other models for that, like Hydrogen.
2. Google created Carbon without caring for inference costs. DeepMind is subsidized by the rest of Google's empire. Selling inference is an insignificant part of Google's revenue. But for Anthropic and OpenAI, selling inference is their entire business model. Anthropic and OpenAI have enormous incentive to sell as much inference as they can in the most efficient manner. Google doesn't have this incentive.

comments.author: noduerme
comments.text:
The composability of jQuery has been an inspiration for the way I design my own frameworks and tools.
One thing I still regularly use jQuery for, though, that's rarely mentioned, is its event model. You can put a listener on any object, not just things in the DOM. Any data object can trigger an event. This is incredibly powerful for isolating logic from DOM elements and events. A frequent use case is for DOM elements to contain a reference to a data object that may be replicated elsewhere on the page. The data object sets up and tears down visual elements, listening for interaction, then dispatches a custom event. Your core logic listens for events on the data object instead of on every individual element that might refer to it. I usually delegate the draw routine for e.g. html snippets of a card or an interactive element to the data object itself in a draw() function that returns a string which incidentally jQuery handles quite nicely inserting into the DOM without needing to explicitly call createElement.

comments.author: colek42
comments.text:
We should probably be measuring deployable merges to main.  The math just doesn't work for pipeline based CI as you add more agents.
Three things matter.
1 -- How many non-conflicting changes can actually be made at one time (Fan Out)
2 -- How long a critical path takes
3 -- How many times you have to run that critical path.  Most orgs run it 2-3x, once before the PR in the agent loop, once in CI, and another in the MQ
This is why most orgs cant get past about 12 PRs an hour.

comments.author: Zigurd
comments.text: I find myself pulled in two directions by the performance of coding agents: First, keeping them on a short leash seems sensible. I don't get failed results very often. When I first started using coding agents, this seemed not just sensible but required in order to not deal with a lot of hallucinated weirdness. Secondly though, it's pretty cool to vaguely wave your hands in a certain direction and get both user interface and business logic that's objectively nicer than I would've gotten from the effort I would've put into manually coding. comments.author: xyzzy_plugh
comments.text:
I don't like this framing.
For a given model, the best harness depends on the problem. As models become increasingly capable, the harness  appears to matter more than the model. This is perhaps controversial but allow me to explain.
Most of my problems are in a single domain, using specific tools and programming languages. I give whatever model de jour the specific tools it needs to solve the problem. I don't let it execute arbitrary scripts or programs (though it can, if it really tries). I give it a restricted number of calls and I feed that information back into it (budget). I let it farm out work to other models, using the same harness. I give everything a budget, which is tracked and enforced, but it's not real, and refills at different times.
This bespoke, specialized harness absolutely smokes any other mainstream harness for these tasks. Significantly faster, cheaper, more correct.
But I can't build a mobile app with this harness, or make a movie.
These tests are doing the same thing. They measure a handful of scenarios. I can't easily tell if those map to my needs or not. In my experience, very few of them do.

comments.author: bisonbear
comments.text:
These are cool results and I'm glad that tokens are being invested to eval harness capabilities.
However, I am hesitant on the correlation between pass/fail in evals which are a binary 0/1 determined by tests, and real world usage, where users can steer, run code review, and care about more than just test pass/fail.
I wrote about the problem of determining "success" for coding agents, and a lot of it boils down to the fact that agents can write dumb code that passes tests, and write smart code that fails tests, and we need to shift to rewarding quality of code and alignment with intent rather than just signal on held out tests (which is still important!)
https://www.stet.sh/blog/cost-per-successful-task
